inputs.original_text: Tens of thousands marched in central London under an “anti-far-right” banner, backed by trade unions, anti-racism groups and Muslim representative bodies. With local elections approaching, the timing looks like an effort to set the boundaries of acceptable opinion before voters have their say. Branding dissent as “far-right” is no substitute for answering people’s concerns about national identity, social order and the traditions that bind communities together. A healthy society should defend open debate, not use political labels to shut it down.
inputs.modified_text: Tens of thousands marched in central London with trade unions, anti-racism groups and Muslim representative bodies—people standing together against far-right politics and the harm it can do to vulnerable communities. Calling that an attempt to silence voters turns collective action into a threat without showing that anyone’s debate is being shut down. People deserve to discuss social and economic concerns, but “open debate” cannot mean giving prejudice a free pass or asking targeted communities to accept it in the name of tradition. The answer is to confront the inequalities and insecurity that fuel division, not to dismiss anti-racist organising as an effort to police opinion.
